summary: Defines a MIB for managing the Baseline Privacy Interface, which provides data privacy for DOCSIS 1.0 cable modems and their termination systems, using SNMP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3083 defines SNMP-readable objects for managing Baseline Privacy in DOCSIS 1.0 cable systems. Operators can inspect key state and related settings on modems and head-end equipment.

subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and configuring DOCSIS 1.0 Baseline Privacy on cable modems and head-end systems.

tldr.problem: Operators need management information about Baseline Privacy settings, keys, state machines, counters, and multicast access in DOCSIS 1.0 cable systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3083 defines the DOCS-BPI-MIB as an SMIv2 module for SNMP management of cable modems and cable modem termination systems.
tldr.outcome: The MIB addresses DOCSIS 1.0 BPI, not BPI+. RFC 3083 has been updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 3083 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 9141. It covers DOCSIS 1.0 Baseline Privacy.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 3083 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). It covers the Baseline Privacy Interface (BPI), which provides data privacy for DOCSIS 1.0 cable modems and cable modem termination systems (CMTSs).

The MIB follows SMIv2 and extends the DOCSIS Radio Frequency Interface MIB. The RFC says CableLabs requires this MIB in DOCSIS 1.0 cable modems that implement BPI. It does not cover BPI+, which is associated with DOCSIS 1.1.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB gives network managers a standard set of SNMP objects for viewing and managing DOCSIS 1.0 privacy information. It covers the modem and the cable company's head-end system, not BPI+.

sections.title: Management Information Operators Need
sections.content:
The requirements call for viewing relevant RSA public keys and the parameters of authorization and Traffic Encryption Key (TEK) state machines. Operators need to see whether privacy is enabled, key lifetimes, grace periods, timeouts, and the current state of a modem's authorization process.

The MIB also exposes error codes and text, counters for invalid key events and renewals, and key sequence numbers and expiration times. On the CMTS, operators need to view and configure multicast forwarding and group membership information.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB provides gauges for key status, errors, and expirations. It also lets operators inspect which modems are allowed to receive shared multicast traffic.

sections.title: Objects for Modems and Head-End Systems
sections.content:
The MIB has one group of objects for cable modems and another for CMTSs. On a modem, the base table contains general privacy parameters, counters, and authorization state. A second table tracks the TEK state machine for each service identifier (SID).

The CMTS objects include base, authorization, and TEK tables, plus two multicast tables. One maps downstream IP multicast traffic to multicast SIDs; the other records which modems may receive each SID. Together they restrict multicast distribution to authorized modems.
sections.plainLanguage: The modem has objects for its main authorization process and its traffic keys. The head-end has matching information for each modem and service, plus tables that control shared channels.

sections.title: Authorization Keys and Traffic Keys
sections.content:
The CMTS sends an authorization key to the modem encrypted with the modem's RSA public key. The authorization key helps derive a key-encryption key that protects TEKs, as well as message-authentication keys. The TEKs are used for DES encryption of upstream and downstream traffic.

Many MIB objects report the current state, sequence number, expiration time, error information, and counters. A modem's grace-time objects report how long before a key expires the modem should begin requesting a replacement. Most modem objects are read-only; the RFC defines a reset object that can trigger reauthorization.
sections.plainLanguage: The authorization key helps protect the traffic keys, and the traffic keys protect cable data. The MIB lets an operator see when keys expire and how the authorization process is going.

sections.title: Protect Management Access
sections.content:
The RFC states that BPI does not provide an authentication service. It advises CMTS implementers not to rely on a modem's MAC address alone for service authorization, particularly for multicast authorization.

Read-write management objects should be protected from unauthorized changes because changes could disrupt service or enable theft of service. The RFC prefers SNMPv3 with its User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control Model. It warns that weaker access controls based on source addresses may be vulnerable to spoofing.
sections.plainLanguage: The privacy interface does not prove who a modem is. Protect the management controls so an unauthorized station cannot change keys or multicast access.
